title: A Balanced Plate
summary: How to build a balanced plate with vegetables and fruit, grains, protein, and dairy, and why each food group matters for a healthy body.
poll: It is fine to eat sweets every day if you also eat vegetables.

versions.title: A Plate With a Bit of All
versions.text:
Your body needs food. But no one food has all it needs. So you need a mix.

Think of your plate. Make it a balanced plate. It has a bit of each kind of food.

Fill half the plate with vegetables and fruit. Pick lots of hues. Red is good. Green is good. They help keep you well.

Fill one fourth with grains. Bread and rice are grains. They give you energy. Then you can run and play. Brown bread keeps you full for a long time.

Fill the last fourth with protein. Fish has it. Eggs and beans do too. It helps build strong muscles.

Milk and cheese are good too. They make bones and teeth strong.

Drink lots of water. It is the best drink. Sweet drinks have lots of sugar.

A bit of oil and nuts is fine. Have sweets just once in a while.

In Saudi Arabia, kabsa has rice and meat. Add a big salad. Now it is a balanced plate! A few dates make a sweet snack.

versions.title: A Plate With a Bit of Everything
versions.text:
Your body needs food to grow and stay well. But no one food has all that your body needs. That is why you need to eat a mix.

Think about your plate. Try to make it a balanced plate. That means it has a bit of each kind of food.

Fill half of your plate with vegetables and fruit. Pick many colors, like red, green, and orange. They help keep you well.

Fill one fourth of your plate with grains. Bread and rice are grains. They give you energy to run and play. Brown bread and oats keep you full for a long time.

Fill the last fourth with protein. Fish, eggs, chicken, and beans all have protein. It helps build strong muscles.

Milk, laban, and cheese are good for you too. They help make strong bones and teeth.

Drink lots of water. It is the best drink. Sweet drinks have lots of sugar in them.

A small bit of oil and nuts is fine. Eat sweets only once in a while.

In Saudi Arabia, kabsa has rice and meat. Add a big salad, and you have a balanced plate. A few dates make a sweet snack!

versions.title: Building a Balanced Plate
versions.text:
Your body needs food to grow and stay well. But no one food has all that your body needs. So it is smart to eat lots of kinds of food.

Here is a good way to plan a meal. Think of your plate. Try to make it a balanced plate. It should have some of each kind of food.

Fill half of your plate with vegetables and fruit. Pick lots of colors. Try red tomatoes, green cucumbers, and orange carrots. Each color helps your body in a different way.

Fill one fourth of your plate with grains. Bread, rice, and oats are grains. They give you energy to run, play, and think. Brown bread and brown rice keep you full for longer.

Fill the last fourth with protein. Fish, eggs, chicken, and beans all have protein. It helps your body build strong muscles. It also helps you heal.

Milk, laban, and cheese are good for you, too. They help build strong bones and teeth.

Water is the best drink. Sweet drinks have lots of sugar. Have them just once in a while.

A little olive oil or a few nuts is good for you. Fried foods and sweets are fine now and then. But do not eat them each day.

In Saudi Arabia, lots of families eat kabsa. It has rice and chicken. Add a big salad, and you have a balanced plate. A few dates make a sweet snack!

versions.title: Building a Balanced Plate
versions.text:
Your body needs food to grow, move, think, and stay well. But no single food has everything your body needs. That is why you should eat many kinds of food each day.

Here is a good way to plan a meal. Picture your plate. Try to make it a balanced plate, with some food from each group.

Fill half of your plate with vegetables and fruit. Pick lots of colors, such as red tomatoes, green cucumbers, and orange carrots. Each color helps your body in a different way. So a bright plate is a healthy plate.

Fill one fourth of your plate with grains, such as bread, rice, or oats. Grains give your body energy to run, play, and think. Brown bread and brown rice keep you full for a longer time.

Fill the last fourth with protein. Fish, eggs, chicken, beans, and lentils are all good choices. Protein helps your body build strong muscles. It also helps your body fix itself when you get hurt.

Milk, laban, and cheese are good for you, too. They help build strong bones and teeth.

Water is the best drink for your body. Sweet drinks have a lot of sugar, so it is smart to have them just once in a while.

A little olive oil or a handful of nuts is good for you. Fried foods and sweets are fine now and then, but not every day.

In Saudi Arabia, many families eat kabsa, which has rice and chicken. If you add a big salad, you have a balanced plate. A few dates make a sweet snack!

versions.title: A Balanced Plate
versions.text:
Your body needs food to grow, move, think, and stay healthy. But no single food has every nutrient your body needs. Nutrients are the useful parts of food, and different foods give you different ones, which is why you should eat many kinds of food each day.

Here is a helpful way to plan a meal. Picture your plate. Try to make it a balanced plate, with food from each main group in the right portion.

Fill half of your plate with vegetables and fruit. Pick many colors, such as red tomatoes, green cucumbers, and orange carrots. These foods provide vitamins and minerals, and they also give you fiber, which helps your body digest food.

Fill one fourth of your plate with grains, such as bread, rice, or oats. Grains are full of carbohydrates, which give you energy to run, play, and think. Whole grains, like brown bread and brown rice, have more fiber, so they keep you full longer.

Fill the last fourth with protein. Fish, eggs, chicken, beans, and lentils are all good choices. Protein helps your body build strong muscles and fix itself.

Milk, laban, and cheese are good too, because they contain calcium, which builds strong bones and teeth.

Water is the best drink. Sweet drinks have a lot of sugar, so have them only once in a while.

A small amount of healthy fat, such as olive oil or nuts, is good for you. Fried foods and sweets are fine now and then, but not every day.

In Saudi Arabia, many families enjoy kabsa, made with rice and chicken. Adding a big salad turns it into a balanced plate, and a few dates make a sweet snack.

versions.title: A Balanced Plate
versions.text:
Your body needs food to grow, move, think, and stay healthy. However, no single food has every nutrient your body needs. Nutrients are the useful substances in food, and different foods supply different ones, which is why it is important to eat many kinds of food each day.

One good way to plan a meal is to picture your plate. Try to make it a balanced plate, with food from each main group in the right portion.

Fill half of your plate with vegetables and fruit. Choose many colors, such as red tomatoes, green cucumbers, and orange carrots. These foods provide vitamins and minerals, and they also supply fiber, which helps your body digest food properly.

Fill one quarter of your plate with grains, such as bread, rice, or oats. Grains are rich in carbohydrates, which give your body energy to run, play, and think. Whole grains, like brown bread and brown rice, have extra fiber, so they keep you feeling full longer.

Fill the last quarter with protein. Fish, eggs, chicken, beans, and lentils are all good sources. Protein helps your body build strong muscles and repair damaged tissue.

Milk, laban, and cheese are also good choices, because they contain calcium, which builds strong bones and teeth.

Water is the best drink. Sugary drinks contain a lot of sugar, so it is wise to have them only now and then.

A small amount of healthy fat, such as olive oil or nuts, is good for you. Fried foods and sweets are fine once in a while, but not every day.

In Saudi Arabia, many families enjoy kabsa, which combines rice and chicken. Adding a big salad turns it into a balanced plate, and a few dates make a sweet, healthy snack.

versions.title: A Balanced Plate
versions.text:
Your body depends on food to grow, move, think, and stay healthy. However, no single food contains every nutrient your body requires. Nutrients are the useful substances in food, and different foods supply different ones. That is why experts say we should eat a variety of foods every day.

One practical way to plan a meal is to picture your plate. The goal is a balanced plate, which has food from each of the main groups in the right portion.

Fill half of your plate with vegetables and fruit, choosing a range of colors, such as red tomatoes, green cucumbers, and orange carrots. These foods provide vitamins, minerals, and fiber, which helps your body digest food properly.

Fill one quarter of your plate with grains, such as bread, rice, or oats. Grains are rich in carbohydrates, which give your body energy for running, playing, and thinking. Whole grains, like brown bread and brown rice, contain extra fiber, so they keep you feeling full longer.

Fill the last quarter with protein. Fish, eggs, chicken, beans, and lentils are all excellent sources. Protein helps your body build strong muscles and repair damaged tissue.

Milk, laban, and cheese are also valuable choices, because they contain calcium, a mineral that builds strong bones and teeth.

Water is the healthiest drink. Sugary drinks contain a surprising amount of sugar, so it is sensible to have them only once in a while.

A small amount of healthy fat, such as olive oil or nuts, is good for your body. Fried foods and sweets are fine occasionally, but not every day.

In Saudi Arabia, many families enjoy kabsa, which combines rice and chicken. Adding a large salad turns it into a balanced plate, and a few dates make a naturally sweet snack.

versions.title: A Balanced Plate
versions.text:
Your body needs food to grow, move, think, and stay healthy. However, no single food contains every nutrient your body requires. Nutrients are the beneficial substances in food, and different foods supply different combinations of them, which is why nutrition experts recommend eating a variety of foods every day.

One practical way to plan a meal is to picture your plate. The objective is a balanced plate, which includes food from each of the principal groups in an appropriate portion.

Fill half of your plate with vegetables and fruit, selecting a range of colors, such as red tomatoes, green cucumbers, and orange carrots. These foods provide vitamins, minerals, and fiber, which helps your body digest food efficiently.

Fill one quarter of your plate with grains, such as bread, rice, or oats. Grains are rich in carbohydrates, which supply your body with energy for running, playing, and concentrating. Whole grains, like brown bread and brown rice, contain additional fiber, so they keep you feeling satisfied considerably longer.

Fill the remaining quarter with protein. Fish, eggs, chicken, beans, and lentils are all excellent sources. Protein helps your body to build strong muscles and repair damaged tissue.

Milk, laban, yogurt, and cheese are also valuable choices, because they contain calcium, a mineral that strengthens bones and teeth.

Water is the healthiest drink. Sugary drinks contain a surprising amount of sugar, so it is sensible to enjoy them only occasionally.

A modest amount of healthy fat, such as olive oil or nuts, benefits your body. Fried foods and sweets are acceptable occasionally, but not on a daily basis.

In Saudi Arabia, many families enjoy kabsa, which combines rice and chicken. Adding a generous salad transforms it into a balanced plate, and a few dates make a naturally sweet, nutritious snack.

versions.title: A Balanced Plate
versions.text:
Your body depends on food to grow, move, think, and remain healthy, yet no single food contains every nutrient your body requires. Nutrients are the beneficial substances in food, and because different foods supply different combinations of them, nutrition experts recommend eating a wide variety of foods every day.

One practical strategy for planning a meal is to visualize your plate. The objective is a balanced plate, which includes food from each of the principal food groups in an appropriate portion.

Vegetables and fruit should fill half of the plate, and choosing a range of colors, such as red tomatoes, green cucumbers, and orange carrots, is wise because each color offers a slightly different mix of vitamins and minerals. These foods also provide fiber, which helps your body digest food efficiently.

Grains, such as bread, rice, or oats, should fill one quarter of the plate. Grains are rich in carbohydrates, your body's main source of energy for running, playing, and concentrating. Whole grains, like brown bread and brown rice, retain more fiber, so they keep you feeling satisfied considerably longer.

Protein should fill the remaining quarter. Fish, eggs, chicken, beans, and lentils are all excellent sources, and protein enables your body to build strong muscles and repair damaged tissue.

Dairy foods, including milk, laban, yogurt, and cheese, are also valuable, because they contain calcium, a mineral that strengthens bones and teeth.

Water is the healthiest beverage, whereas sugary drinks contain a surprising quantity of sugar and are best enjoyed only occasionally.

Healthy fats, such as olive oil or nuts, benefit your body in small amounts. Fried foods and sweets are acceptable in moderation, meaning occasionally rather than daily.

In Saudi Arabia, many families enjoy kabsa, which combines rice and chicken. Adding a generous salad transforms it into a balanced plate, and a few dates make a naturally sweet, nutritious snack.

versions.title: A Balanced Plate
versions.text:
Your body depends on food to grow, move, think, and remain healthy, yet no single food contains every nutrient your body requires. Nutrients are the beneficial substances in food, and because different foods supply different combinations of them, nutrition experts consistently recommend eating a wide variety of foods every day.

One practical strategy for planning a meal is to visualize your plate. The objective is a balanced plate, which incorporates food from each of the principal food groups in an appropriate portion.

Vegetables and fruit should occupy half of the plate, and selecting a range of colors, such as red tomatoes, green cucumbers, and orange carrots, is sensible because each color offers a slightly different combination of vitamins and minerals. These foods additionally provide fiber, which helps your body digest food efficiently.

Grains, such as bread, rice, or oats, should occupy one quarter of the plate. Grains are rich in carbohydrates, your body's primary source of energy for running, playing, and concentrating. Whole grains, like brown bread and brown rice, retain considerably more fiber, so they keep you feeling satisfied substantially longer.

Protein should occupy the remaining quarter. Fish, eggs, chicken, beans, and lentils are all excellent sources, and protein enables your body to construct strong muscles and repair damaged tissue.

Dairy foods, including milk, laban, yogurt, and cheese, are also valuable, because they contain calcium, a mineral that strengthens bones and teeth.

Water is the healthiest beverage, whereas sugary drinks contain a surprising quantity of sugar and are best enjoyed only occasionally.

Healthy fats, such as olive oil or nuts, benefit your body in small amounts. Fried foods and sweets are acceptable in moderation, meaning occasionally rather than daily.

Balance also applies to the whole day rather than to every single meal. If your lunch contains few vegetables, for instance, you can compensate by including additional vegetables at dinner, and a piece of fruit makes an excellent snack between meals.

In Saudi Arabia, many families enjoy kabsa, which combines rice and chicken. Adding a generous salad transforms it into a balanced plate, and a few dates provide a naturally sweet, nutritious snack.

versions.title: A Balanced Plate
versions.text:
Your body depends on food to grow, move, think, and remain healthy, yet no single food contains every nutrient your body requires. Nutrients are the beneficial substances in food, and because different foods supply different combinations of them, nutrition experts consistently recommend consuming a wide variety of foods every day.

One practical strategy for planning a meal is to visualize your plate. The objective is a balanced plate, which incorporates food from each of the principal food groups in an appropriate portion.

Vegetables and fruit should occupy half of the plate, and selecting a range of colors, such as red tomatoes, green cucumbers, and orange carrots, is sensible because each color offers a slightly different combination of vitamins and minerals. These foods additionally provide fiber, which helps your body digest food efficiently and regularly.

Grains, such as bread, rice, or oats, should occupy one quarter of the plate. Grains are abundant in carbohydrates, your body's primary source of energy for running, playing, and concentrating. Whole grains, like brown bread and brown rice, retain considerably more fiber, so they keep you feeling satisfied substantially longer than refined white varieties.

Protein should occupy the remaining quarter. Fish, eggs, chicken, beans, and lentils are all excellent sources, and protein enables your body to construct strong muscles and repair damaged tissue.

Dairy foods, including milk, laban, yogurt, and cheese, are also valuable, because they contain calcium, a mineral that strengthens bones and teeth.

Water is unquestionably the healthiest beverage, whereas sugary drinks contain a surprising quantity of sugar and are therefore best enjoyed only occasionally.

Healthy fats, such as olive oil or nuts, benefit your body in small amounts, while fried foods and sweets are acceptable in moderation, meaning occasionally rather than habitually.

Balance additionally applies to the entire day rather than to every individual meal. If your lunch contains relatively few vegetables, for instance, you can compensate by including additional vegetables at dinner, and a piece of fresh fruit constitutes an excellent snack between meals.

In Saudi Arabia, many families enjoy kabsa, which combines rice and chicken, and adding a generous salad transforms it into a balanced plate, and a few dates provide a naturally sweet, nutritious snack.

versions.title: A Balanced Plate
versions.text:
Your body depends on food to grow, move, think, and remain healthy, yet no single food contains every nutrient your body requires. Nutrients are the beneficial substances in food, and because different foods supply different combinations of them, nutrition specialists consistently recommend consuming a wide variety of foods every day.

One practical strategy for planning a nutritious meal is to visualize your plate. The objective is a balanced plate, which incorporates food from each of the principal food groups in an appropriate portion.

Vegetables and fruit should occupy half of the plate, and selecting a diverse range of colors, such as red tomatoes, green cucumbers, and orange carrots, is sensible because each color offers a slightly different combination of vitamins and minerals. These foods additionally provide dietary fiber, which helps your body digest food efficiently and regularly.

Grains, such as bread, rice, or oats, should occupy one quarter of the plate. Grains are abundant in carbohydrates, your body's primary source of energy for running, playing, and concentrating. Whole grains, like brown bread and brown rice, retain considerably more fiber, so they keep you feeling satisfied substantially longer than refined white varieties.

Protein should occupy the remaining quarter, and fish, eggs, chicken, beans, and lentils are all excellent sources; protein enables your body to construct strong muscles and repair damaged tissue.

Furthermore, dairy foods, including milk, laban, yogurt, and cheese, are also valuable, because they contain calcium, an essential mineral that strengthens bones and teeth.

Water is unquestionably the healthiest beverage, whereas sugary drinks contain a surprising quantity of sugar and are therefore best enjoyed only occasionally.

Healthy fats, such as olive oil or nuts, benefit your body in limited amounts, whereas fried foods and confectionery are acceptable in moderation, meaning occasionally rather than habitually.

Importantly, balance applies to the entire day rather than exclusively to every individual meal, so if your lunch contains relatively few vegetables, you can compensate by incorporating additional vegetables at dinner, and a piece of fresh fruit or a small bowl of yogurt constitutes an excellent, convenient snack between meals.

In Saudi Arabia, many families enjoy kabsa, which traditionally combines rice and chicken or lamb, and adding a generous salad transforms it into a balanced plate, and a few dates provide a naturally sweet, nutritious snack.

keyWords.definition: having the right amount of each part
keyWords.example: Our team has a balanced mix of fast runners and strong defenders.

keyWords.definition: plants or parts of plants that people eat, such as carrots and cucumbers
keyWords.example: Grandma grows tomatoes and other vegetables on her roof.

keyWords.definition: the power your body needs to move, play, and think
keyWords.example: After a good night's sleep, Salem had lots of energy for the trip.

keyWords.definition: a part of food, found in fish, eggs, meat, and beans, that helps the body grow
keyWords.example: Lentil soup is a warm meal with plenty of protein.

keyWords.definition: the parts of the body that help you move and lift
keyWords.example: Swimming makes the muscles in your arms stronger.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to cook kabsa for a big family
Why water is the best drink to have
How to make a healthy plate of food
questions.why: The article explains how to make a balanced plate with a bit of each kind of food.

wrong.A: Kabsa is named at the end, but the article does not tell how to cook it.
wrong.B: Water is named, but its temperature is not discussed.
wrong.D: The article says to eat sweets only once in a while.

questions.stem: How much of the plate should be vegetables and fruit?
questions.why: The article says to fill half the plate with vegetables and fruit.

wrong.B: The article says vegetables and fruit should be a big part of the plate.
wrong.C: One fourth is for grains or for protein.
wrong.D: Then there would be no room for grains or protein.

questions.stem: Which food helps build strong muscles?
options: Sweet drinks with lots of sugar
questions.why: Fish and eggs have protein, and the article says protein helps build strong muscles.

wrong.A: Sweet drinks have lots of sugar, not protein.
wrong.C: Candy is a sweet to have only once in a while.
wrong.D: A bit of oil is fine, but it is not named for muscles.

questions.stem: What do grains like bread and rice give you?
questions.why: The article says grains give you energy so you can run and play.

wrong.C: Colors are talked about for vegetables and fruit.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: "Make it a balanced plate." What does balanced mean here?
options: Having a bit of each kind of food
Holding the plate up high on one finger
Having only one kind of food
questions.why: The article explains that a balanced plate has a bit of each kind of food.

wrong.B: That is a different meaning of balance.
wrong.C: This is the opposite of a balanced plate.
wrong.D: The word is about what is on the plate, not speed.

questions.stem: Hamad drinks three sweet drinks every day. What would the article most likely tell him?
options: Sweet drinks are the best drink.
He should stop drinking any water.
questions.why: The article says water is the best drink and that sweet drinks have lots of sugar.

wrong.A: The article says water is the best drink.
wrong.B: The article tells you to drink lots of water.
wrong.D: Milk and cheese help bones, not sweet drinks.

questions.stem: A family eats kabsa with rice and meat. What could they add to make a balanced plate?
questions.why: The article says adding a big salad to kabsa makes a balanced plate, because half the plate should be vegetables.

wrong.A: The kabsa already has rice, which is a grain.
wrong.C: Sweet drinks have lots of sugar.
wrong.D: The kabsa already has meat, which is protein.

questions.stem: Why does the author split the plate into parts in the article?
options: To show how to wash and dry dishes
To tell a story about a family
To compare plates from many countries
To show how much of each food to eat
questions.why: Splitting the plate into half and fourths shows readers how much of each kind of food to choose.

wrong.A: Washing dishes is not in the article.
wrong.B: The article gives facts, not a story.
wrong.C: Plates from other countries are not compared.

LOW.prompt: Draw or describe a balanced plate for your lunch. Tell what goes in each part and why.
checklist: I put vegetables and fruit in half of the plate.
I added a grain and a protein food.
I said why one food is good for my body.

Eating many food groups gives the body what it needs.
Children should never eat any fried food at all.
Kabsa is the healthiest meal in the world.

wrong.A: Grains give energy, but the article is about many groups.
wrong.C: The article says fried foods are fine occasionally.
wrong.D: Kabsa is an example, not the main idea.

It helps the body digest food.

wrong.B: Bread and rice are grains with carbohydrates.
wrong.D: These are vegetables named for vitamins and fiber.

wrong.C: The article does not describe cooking.

By food group and what each group does
As a list of questions and answers
As a comparison of foods in two countries

wrong.C: It is not written as questions and answers.

wrong.A: Calcium comes from milk, laban, and cheese.
wrong.B: Protein comes from fish, eggs, chicken, and beans.
wrong.D: She is not eating any vegetables.

I named at least two nutrients, such as fiber or calcium.
I explained what each nutrient does for the body.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?

Sweets should never be eaten by anyone, at any time.
Protein is the body's main source of energy.
Different food groups, in sensible amounts, meet the body's needs.

wrong.B: The article says sweets are acceptable in moderation.
wrong.C: The article names carbohydrates as the main energy source.

questions.stem: The article says fried foods and sweets are acceptable "in moderation." What does this phrase mean?

Only when eaten together with vegetables

questions.stem: Why does the author end with the example of kabsa and a salad?

questions.stem: A student's lunch is a large plate of white rice with a small piece of chicken. What change would best follow the article's advice?

wrong.B: The article says nothing like this.
wrong.D: Sweetness is not the reason given.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say, "As long as I eat vegetables, I can eat sweets every day." Use the article to explain whether you agree or disagree.
